entities.name: Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus (c. 64 BCE – 8 CE) was a pivotal Roman statesman, military commander, orator, and a preeminent patron of arts and letters during the tumultuous transition from the Roman Republic to the Augustan Principate. A scion of the ancient Valerian gens, his career spanned the civil wars following Caesar's assassination and the consolidation of Octavian's power, positioning him at the intersection of political ambition and cultural renaissance. Messalla Corvinus embodied the ideal of the cultivated Roman aristocrat, wielding influence not only on the battlefield and in the Senate but also through his sophisticated literary circle, which rivaled that of Maecenas. His life and work offer a crucial lens into the intellectual and political currents that shaped the early Roman Empire.

Initially a staunch republican who fought against Octavian at Philippi in 42 BCE, Messalla Corvinus displayed remarkable political pragmatism and military acumen, eventually reconciling with Octavian (later Augustus) and becoming one of his most trusted generals. He served as consul in 31 BCE, the same year as the Battle of Actium, though he was not present at the decisive naval engagement. His military achievements included suppressing a revolt in Aquitania in 28 BCE, for which he celebrated a triumph, and holding significant commands in Syria. Beyond his martial prowess, Messalla Corvinus was renowned for his oratorical skill, considered second only to Cicero by some contemporaries, and his administrative integrity, notably as curator aquarum (superintendent of the water supply) in 11 BCE.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus played a crucial role in consolidating the Augustan Principate through his military and administrative service, while also fostering a significant literary circle that shaped the 'Golden Age' of Latin literature.
